title: METR RCT (2025)
finding: Experienced developers forecast they would be 24% faster with AI but were measured 19% slower (16 developers, 246 tasks on familiar repos, Claude 3.5/3.7).

title: Anthropic internal study
finding: Engineers fully delegate 0-20% of their work.

title: METR survey
finding: Median value uplift was 1.4-2x against 3x speed, and every checkable 10x claim was overstated.

title: DORA 2025
finding: Delivery instability rises with AI adoption, while small batches amplified product performance and reduced friction (survey of about 5,000).

title: Mathews & Nagappan, ASE 2024
finding: Failed fixes piled up: no problem was solved on attempt 5 (GPT-4, Llama 3).

title: Chen et al., Self-Debugging
finding: The same debugging loop gained 2-3 points with no unit tests (text-to-SQL) and up to 12 points with them (C++ to Python, Codex 80.4% to 92.5%), a bare 'the code is wrong' message gained less than execution results wherever tests existed, and it matched baselines that drew 10 times more samples.

title: Madaan et al., Self-Refine
finding: Self-feedback improved 7 unlike tasks by about 20% absolute on average, but on math ChatGPT judged 94% of its own answers 'everything looks good' and an outside wrong-answer signal added over 5 points; partly GPT-4-judged, no equal-cost baseline.

title: Shinn et al., Reflexion
finding: With no tests, a reflection loop scored below no loop at all (0.52 vs 0.60), a small open model gained nothing (0.26 before and after), and no equal-cost baseline was reported.

title: SWE-agent, NeurIPS 2024
finding: Failed runs cost twice as much as successful ones and more budget rarely rescued them, while collapsing old observations and adding a lint guardrail each lifted solve rate from 15% to 18% (GPT-4 Turbo).

title: METR research update (2025-08)
finding: An agent passed 38% of maintainer test suites, but 0 of 15 reviewed PRs were mergeable, including 4 that passed every test (Claude 3.7).

title: Uber efficient software factory
finding: Cost per session fell 52% with compaction, default effort levels, caching and spend nudges.

title: Databricks, managing AI coding costs
finding: Routing cut task cost by over 30%.

title: Willison, the lethal trifecta
finding: About 15 vendor products whose agents combined private data, untrusted input and an outbound channel were exploited in 2023-2025.

title: LoopsBench
finding: The best result on 112 long tasks was 25.0% resolved (Opus 4.7 in Claude Code with an outer continuation loop, 17.0% without), regressions occurred in all four loop profiles, and the same model (gpt-5.4) scored from 18.75% in Codex down to 7.14% in mini-swe-agent, with the Ralph loop at 7.84% against 24.11% for dynamic workflows; Microsoft authors, tasks built with Claude Code.

title: SWE-Gym, ICML 2025
finding: A verifier trained on agent runs raised SWE-bench Verified from 20.6% (one attempt) to 32.0% (best of 16), but the right patch was often produced and not picked (fine-tuned Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, late-2024 open model).

title: SWE-Search, ICLR 2025
finding: Tree search added 4.0 to 6.7 points on SWE-bench Lite at 5 to 14 times the cost but only 0.6 to 5.3 points at matched compute, and a value function picked the right solution 73% of the time against 84% for a debate between final candidates (GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama 3.1 70B).

title: Jain, are harnesses worth the cost (martinfowler.com)
finding: On one Java service scored by 178 hidden acceptance tests, a test-feedback harness took a cost-optimised model from 3 of 10 to 10 of 10 accepted at 3.9 times the tokens, while a flagship model was 10 of 10 either way at 10.5 times the tokens with the harness; the author founded the company whose tool built the harness.

title: Ralph playbook
finding: Permission-bypass flags leave the sandbox as the only boundary.

title: Fortune on Uber AI spending
finding: Uber used its whole 2026 AI-coding budget in four months after a usage leaderboard.

title: SlopCodeBench
finding: Code quality decays as agents extend their own work, and quality-aware prompts change the starting point but not the rate.

title: Cooper, driving in gears
finding: Proposes stopping after each test when unsure, running several tasks when sure, and keeping auth and payments in low gear; untested.

title: Osmani, software factories
finding: Heuristics that agents hold up for 3-10 steps and drift past 20, and that a loop earns unattended running with a cheap, frequent, hard-to-fake check.

title: Huntley, Ralph
finding: Advises resetting context every loop and using a single validation agent for cleaner signal.

title: Dan Luu, PL tokens
finding: Continuing context did better per unit cost than resetting (n=1 task).

title: Augmented coding patterns catalog
finding: Catalog patterns Overnight Batch and Smart Plan, Cheap Execution propose running low-risk work overnight and having the strongest model plan while a cheaper one executes; no data.

title: Anthropic, effective harnesses for long-running agents
finding: Proposes a JSON feature list where only the passes field is editable to stop premature completion claims.

title: HumanLayer, software factory write-up
finding: A no-review factory was abandoned after about three unrecoverable failures (one company).

title: Böckeler, sensors for coding agents
finding: Proposes sensors at four cadences: in-session, CI, scheduled and production.

title: Uber on Pragmatic Engineer
finding: Uber bundles simple CI jobs into one command the agent runs before opening a PR, after CI jobs more than doubled in a year; self-report.

title: Anthropic, solving code review at Anthropic
finding: The Claude Code team has the agent show test or build output, then a fresh-context subagent reviews the diff before any PR; the 'two to three times better' figure is one engineer's estimate.

title: Fornasier, getting out of the loop
finding: The bottleneck moves to task definition (n=1).

title: Zechner, slowing down
finding: Removing the human bottleneck removes the pain signal.

title: Karpathy on Dwarkesh (2025-10)
finding: Agents were not net useful for novel, precisely arranged code, pushing standard patterns, defensive bloat and deprecated APIs, but helped with boilerplate and a tested port to an unfamiliar language (n=1).

title: Anthropic, the advisor strategy
finding: A cheap model consulting a strong advisor gained 2.7 points on SWE-bench Multilingual at 11.9% less cost per task.

title: Emanuel, overprompting
finding: Uses a plan-then-execute split but insists on an overpowered executor; opinion.

title: Morris, humans and agents
finding: Humans work 'on the loop', changing the specs, checks and guidance that steer the agent rather than the artefact when results are wrong; conceptual, no data.

title: Boeckeler, local models for coding
finding: A locally run 35B mixture-of-experts model handled scripts and small well-specified changes but fell apart on complex logic, and one task failed 5 of 7 automated reruns on one machine (two tasks, one evaluator).

title: PostHog, scheduled agents
finding: A flaky-test agent checking every 3 hours filed 72 reports since July, 11 of which (about 15%) led to merged fixes, while agent-sent tool-feedback reports ran to a few thousand, too many to read; vendor self-report.

title: Bean et al., NeurIPS 2025
finding: Of 445 LLM benchmarks, 16.0% used any statistical test or uncertainty estimate to compare models, 53.4% gave evidence that they measure what they claim, and under 10% used complete real-world tasks.

title: SWE-Bench+
finding: 31.1% of passed SWE-bench patches were suspicious because the tests were weak (reported secondhand via TDD-Bench Verified).

title: TDD-Bench Verified (IBM)
finding: Cited for weak graders: it relays the SWE-Bench+ figure, and the same row reports that 44 of 500 (8.8%) SWE-bench Verified golden tests weren't fail-to-pass or covered no changed lines.

title: Stanford AI Index 2026
finding: Secondary synthesis: invalid benchmark questions ranged from 2% (MMLU Math) to 42% (GSM8K).

title: Peng et al.
finding: Developers were 55.8% faster on one greenfield task, counting only the 35 of 95 who finished; GitHub and Microsoft authors.

title: Harness
finding: A before/after study (n=50) by a vendor of engineering metrics found 10.6% more PRs with Copilot, with no quality data.

title: GitHub blog (Copilot code quality)
finding: Unsigned vendor post with no paper: 13.6% more lines per readability error with Copilot, reviewed only by the 25 developers whose code passed every test.

title: Imai, ICSE 2022 poster
finding: A 20-person student poster (abstract only) found lower quality with Copilot pairing.

title: Pearce et al., IEEE S&P 2022
finding: About 40% of completions for risky scenarios were vulnerable.

title: Meta CTO post via Reuters and Ars Technica
finding: Per an internal CTO post reported secondhand, code changes at Meta rose 220% while user-facing feature changes rose 36%.

title: Guardian
finding: Reports secondhand a WSJ survey of 5,000 in which 92% of executives say AI makes them more productive and 40% of non-managers say it saves no time; its account of the Liebscher study gives 1,150 workers and 40% exposure, a discrepancy the doc calls unexplained.

title: Liebscher et al.
finding: In a self-report preprint (n=962, BetterUp and Stanford authors), 52.7% said they had sent AI work they judged low quality; 38% received some in the last month and spent 3.3-3.4 hours a month on it; 36% then wanted to avoid that colleague.

title: Cursor telemetry via Orosz
finding: One model cost about 2x another per agent request but tied per accepted line; Orosz notes Cursor gains if its own model looks cheap.

title: PostHog newsletter
finding: With no methodology given, a daily bill doubled ($5k to $10k) while cost per run fell ($1.80 to $1.40), and a cheaper model was 20% cheaper in one test, not the 2.5x its list price suggests, because it took 1.7x the turns.

title: Tabarsi et al.
finding: Of 16 early adopters interviewed, 14 reported less mundane work and 13 saved time, yet 8 discarded most generated code and 15 modified code before using it.

title: Orosz, ROI of AI spend
finding: Vendor data shows weekly PRs up 113% and monthly PRs up 127% year on year among CodeRabbit users; interviews across 27 companies found spend from under $300 to $3,000+ per developer per month and PR change from flat to 5-10x, with one company's PR size tripling while count stayed flat.

title: SAGA, NeurIPS 2025
finding: Solutions that passed LiveCodeBench's private tests failed on LeetCode 20% (medium) and 40% (hard) of the time.

title: VERINA, ICLR 2026
finding: Almost all code failures in this Lean 4 benchmark were compile errors (o3: 25.8 of 27.4 points), so its code score mostly measures writing Lean that compiles.

title: ICONIQ State of AI 2026
finding: Executives report about 31% time savings from coding assistance (executive self-report, n=247).

title: Raicea, PostHog
finding: Claims boolean LLM judges with concrete examples are reliable enough, with no agreement data, and recommends observing, curating failures into evals, sampling 5-10% of traffic and reviewing traces weekly.

title: Anderson
finding: Newsletter forecast with no data: steering people to cheaper models can raise retries and human correction and erase the saving.

title: Forbes
finding: Reports secondhand that Amazon withdrew an internal usage leaderboard after staff gamed it.

title: Ludic
finding: Anonymous testimony that engineers under quotas ran self-prompting loops and none was caught.

title: Chatterji et al. (OpenAI)
finding: OpenAI's own working paper on ChatGPT Enterprise says message volume measures intensity, not economic importance.

title: Business Insider
finding: Reports that Duolingo dropped AI usage from performance reviews.

title: Ewerlof
finding: Essay by a critic of AI mandates, anecdotes only: token usage as a productivity proxy is a vanity metric.

title: Honeycomb
finding: A CTO describes an unmeasured company policy: say what an artifact is, why you send it and how much review you want.

title: Bean, Strauss & Singh, HBR
finding: Prescriptive: keep separate scorecards for human, agent and combined system.

title: pinecoder
finding: One engineer reports about 3x merged PRs after a model upgrade, with method and baseline not shown (personal essay, n=1).

title: Gloaguen et al.
finding: LLM-generated context files lowered success slightly and raised cost 20-23%, hand-written ones gave +2.4% over no file (p=0.21) with cost up to 19%, repo overviews did not help agents find files, and tools named in a context file were used 1.6 times per task against under 0.01 otherwise, with reasoning tokens up 10-22% (GPT-5.x and Sonnet 4.5).

title: Lulla et al., ICSE workshop 2026
finding: A short AGENTS.md cut median time 28.6% and output tokens 16.6% with gpt-5.2-codex; correctness was not measured.

title: Shim et al., ICLR 2026
finding: Performance peaked well below full context, so more context can be worse (GPT-4o, Qwen 2.5).

title: Paulsen
finding: Retrieval degraded with length: most models degraded severely by 1,000 tokens.

title: Galster et al., AIware '26
finding: In 2,853 engineered GitHub repositories, 90.6% had a context file (CLAUDE.md in 45.9% and AGENTS.md in 39.5% of those), skills and subagents were rare and mostly static text, and 301 of 497 context-file pointer pairs pointed from CLAUDE.md to AGENTS.md; this measures adoption, not benefit.

title: Paltenghi & Chandra, arXiv 2607.09900 (AfterVibe)
finding: A spec recovered from a finished session let a fresh agent rebuild the change at a mean 5.06 of 6 on 72 internal Meta tasks (5.74 after up to three refinement rounds) against 4.23 for the developer's own change description, with specs about 5.7 times shorter than the diff; LLM graders, internal data.

title: STALE
finding: The best model scored 55.2% on acting on updated facts.

title: Rathje et al.
finding: Users rated sycophantic bots as more objective, and 72% of real ChatGPT turns were as agreeable as the sycophantic condition.

title: Anthropic AI-native SDLC playbook
finding: Advises planning before code and committing the plan, and says a skill makes violations rare while a hook makes them close to impossible; untested.

title: Augmented coding obstacles: Selective Hearing
finding: Rules that fight the model's training silently revert.

title: Dodell
finding: Skills should carry novel information or code.

title: LangChain, anatomy of an agent harness
finding: Load skill bodies only when they are used.

title: Kassner & Schütze, ACL 2020
finding: Negations prime the concept they ask the model to avoid (BERT).

title: Min et al., EMNLP 2022
finding: Format and coverage of few-shot examples matter more than correct labels (GPT-3 era).

title: System Design newsletter, spec-driven development
finding: Advises splitting unknowns from assumptions in specs; vendor-sponsored, no data.

title: Margalit et al.
finding: An automated contradiction detector superseded 90 of 90 admitted conflicting facts in one service.

title: Piskala
finding: Keep the spec in sync with code through tests for long-lived systems, use the least rigour that removes ambiguity, and skip specs for exploratory work; no data, and its 'up to 50%' error cut is secondhand and unverified.

title: Ewerlof's pattern catalogue
finding: Proposes loading the whole working set into context instead of retrieving chunks (CAG) for full recall; no data, partly drafted with Gemini.

title: Kohler, NN/g: three agent context roles
finding: A qualitative study with Claude power users proposes asking whether each context item is global (rarely changes), local (one task) or ambient (raw streams).

title: Kohler, NN/g: big ball of mud
finding: Without sorting context by role, nontechnical builders' agent systems grow as big balls of mud.

title: Moran & Gibbons, NN/g: vibe architects
finding: The sample behind the big-ball-of-mud observation is 7 people.

title: Foote & Yoder, 1997
finding: Origin of the term 'big ball of mud', which the authors call a pattern, not an antipattern.

title: Perez, NN/g: context architecture
finding: Position paper arguing for information architecture for context; argued, not measured.

title: Neo Kim and Gencay, Claude Code token usage
finding: Advises starting a new conversation when compaction fires every few messages or earlier rules are forgotten, carrying over a short hand-off summary and keeping standing rules in CLAUDE.md; sponsored, no data.

title: Fowler, 2026-09-28
finding: Argues for hacking until something works, recovering a spec from the session and regenerating to see what the spec kept; a first spec is always wrong and regenerating a bug keeps the bug.

title: Gonzalez, 2026-03
finding: A spec detailed enough to generate software is thinly veiled code, so specs are not cheaper than code; its evidence is one author, one spec, one Claude Code run.

title: Marin-Perez, 2026-05-20
finding: Most projects are well defined but poorly specified, so agents can run free only where any decent output will do; no data, author sells consultancy and training.

title: Boeckeler, three spec-driven development tools
finding: A spec tool turned a small bug into 4 user stories and 16 acceptance criteria, and reviewing many verbose spec files was worse than reviewing code (one evaluator, 2025).

title: Lopopolo, OpenAI harness engineering
finding: One big instruction file failed, so the team kept a short AGENTS.md as a table of contents over structured docs and enforced rules with custom linters; unmeasured, output figures are self-estimates.

title: Demirer et al., NBER w35275
finding: Across 100,000+ developers, AI tools raised lines of code 17.3x and releases only 1.3x; calibrated on this data, unlimited code generation would lift releases only about 10% (a calibration, not an estimate).

title: Faros, 22k devs
finding: Correlational vendor data shows median review time up 441%, incidents per PR up 243% and unreviewed merges up 31%.

title: Perry et al., CCS 2023
finding: AI-assisted participants (n=47) wrote less secure code on 4 of 5 security tasks and were more likely to believe it was secure.

title: Osmani, Agentic code review (CodeRabbit data and multi-tool study)
finding: Relays CodeRabbit data on 470 PRs (Dec 2025) showing 1.7x more issues and 1.5-2x more security issues in AI PRs, and an unnamed study where 93.4% of flagged locations across 146 PRs came from exactly one of four tools (secondhand).

title: He et al., via Ehsani et al.
finding: After Cursor adoption, static-analysis warnings rose 30% and complexity 41% (secondhand).

title: CircleCI, 28 million workflows
finding: Main-branch success fell to 70.8%, a five-year low (no methodology given).

title: Orosz, What is happening with code reviews
finding: GitHub PR volume rose about 5x in three years, and a 5-person team routing risky changes to humans and the rest to AI review went from 80 to 154 PRs per week (self-reported).

title: Baltes et al.
finding: One team handled 30 PRs a day across six reviewers.

title: Vicente & Matute, via Lovett
finding: 80.7% of participants spotted a flawed AI recommendation and followed it anyway.

title: Orosz, The Pulse: concern about AI review
finding: Uber filters AI review comments by confidence and merges duplicates.

title: Evil Martians, Ten anti-AI-slop moves
finding: Recommends phasing deterministic gates: baseline, then warnings on changed files, then blocking.

title: Brasil, When I reject AI code even if it works
finding: Rejects green code the author cannot explain.

title: Tanna, Hand-write commits
finding: Advocates hand-writing commit messages.

title: Lawson, You can just choose how many bugs you want
finding: Without a simplification pass, each bug gets its own patch.

title: Dan Luu, AI coding
finding: Proposes QA and fuzzing instead of default diff review.

title: Tornhill, Controlling the uncertainty machine
finding: Bug fixes get light inspection and novel features deeper structural review, never full line-by-line reading; each review finding becomes an agent skill (his company sells code-health tooling).

title: Cervera, Vibe everything
finding: A human in the loop whose only acceptable answer is approval is there to take the blame, without the knowledge, time or authority to stop a failure (opinion, no data).

title: Ellens, The system is on the other side
finding: Generated tests and AI reviewers each add an interpretation between the engineer and the running system, and AI quality gates turn those interpretations into decisions (no data).

title: Astrogator (UIUC and IBM)
finding: With a user-confirmed formal query and a verifier, 82.9% of correct Ansible programs were accepted and 92.4% of wrong ones rejected, but 68 of 70 wrong accepts traced to queries that left details open, and the human review step was never run (authors' own 21 tasks).

title: Anthropic and Theorem, formal verification
finding: Claude proved 239 OSS-Fuzz entry points crash-free with specs from existing fuzz harnesses, yet one harness asserted less than the post claims.

title: OpenAI, Scaling code verification
finding: OpenAI says its Codex reviewer caught more critical issues with fewer false alarms once given repository access and execution, that 52.7% of its comments led to a code change across over 100k PRs a day, and that recall fell faster on model-written code (figures not reproduced).

title: OWASP LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection
finding: OWASP says it is unclear if there are fool-proof methods of prevention; RAG and fine-tuning don't fully mitigate it, and detecting injected text is an open problem.

title: Role confusion, ICML 2026
finding: Models judge who is speaking by writing style, not role tags; forged reasoning raised attack success from about 0% to 60%.

title: CaMeL, Debenedetti et al.
finding: Isolating untrusted data from planning and checking each tool call against a policy blocked nearly all AgentDojo attacks, solving 77% of tasks vs 84% undefended at about 2.8x the tokens; spotlighting alone cut Claude 3.5 Sonnet's successful attacks from 44 to 5 of 949, with no guarantee and no adaptive attack tested (preprint, Google authors who also built the benchmark).

title: OWASP community, MCP Tool Poisoning
finding: A malicious MCP server's tool responses carry instructions the agent follows; tools are reviewed at connect time but responses are trusted at runtime (no incidence data).

title: MCPTox, Wang et al.
finding: Poisoned tool descriptions succeeded on 36.5% of test cases on average and up to 72.8% across 20 model settings, with refusals under 3%; reasoning mode raised attack success (Qwen3 32B: 58.5% vs 23.7%). Measures susceptibility, not real-world incidence, and tested no defences.

title: OWASP LLM02:2025 Sensitive Information Disclosure
finding: The OWASP category the tab maps the lethal trifecta and credential exposure to.

title: Mollick, opinionated guide
finding: Approve anything that sends, spends or deletes.

title: OWASP LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency
finding: Root causes are excessive functionality, permissions and autonomy; logging and rate limits limit damage but don't prevent it.

title: OWASP LLM07:2025 System Prompt Leakage
finding: System prompts should be treated as extractable.

title: OWASP LLM08:2025 Vector and Embedding Weaknesses
finding: Embeddings can be inverted to recover text, shared stores leak across permission boundaries, and indexed documents can carry hidden instructions.

title: OWASP LLM04:2025 Data and Model Poisoning
finding: Tampered models, LoRA adapters and poisoned data; backdoors can lie dormant.

title: Spracklen et al., USENIX Security 2025
finding: At least 5.2% of packages suggested by commercial models and 21.7% by open-source models didn't exist, about 45% of fake names recurred every time, and checking names against the registry is 'the illusion of verification' once an attacker registers the name.

title: Krishna et al., preprint
finding: Across 11 code models, package hallucination ranged from 0.22% to 46.15% per model and language (5.42% for GPT-4o); larger, higher-scoring models invented fewer packages, a directional result driven partly by two outliers (three of four authors at NVIDIA, whose model scored best).

title: Aikido, slopsquatting
finding: A squatted fake package name got 30,000+ downloads in three months (Lasso), and one spread to 237 repos through LLM-generated agent skills.

title: OWASP LLM09:2025 Misinformation
finding: The OWASP category, including overreliance, that the tab maps slopsquatting, insecure code and skill loss to.

title: OWASP LLM03:2025 Supply Chain
finding: Covers tampered models and packages; vendors can change terms to train on customer data.

title: OWASP A03:2025 Software Supply Chain Failures
finding: The web Top 10 category the tab cites for agent-picked dependencies.

title: OWASP Software Supply Chain Security cheat sheet
finding: Recommends SBOMs, signed sources, pinned registries and egress controls on fetches.

title: OWASP LLM05:2025 Improper Output Handling
finding: Model output is passed to shells, SQL or browsers without validation; a coding agent's shell tool does this by design.

title: OWASP LLM10:2025 Unbounded Consumption
finding: Pay-per-use pricing can be exploited; OWASP favours rate limits, quotas, timeouts and iteration caps.

title: NYT, Anthropic copyright settlement
finding: Anthropic agreed a $1.5B copyright settlement.

title: Aikido SafeChain
finding: A wrapper around npm, npx, yarn and pnpm that checks installs against a malware feed.

title: Geng et al., CMC 2026
finding: A review of 128 studies claims an input filter plus output validation plus model-level defences brings attack success under 5%, but the section it points to reports no measurement.

title: Times of Israel, AI-flagged cargo (CNN relay)
finding: Relays a CNN exclusive that an intelligence report partly produced with AI nearly led to an armed boarding of a ship; unnamed sources, no official confirmation.

title: Trending Topics, false AI intelligence report (CNN relay)
finding: Relays the same CNN exclusive about an AI-assisted intelligence report and a near-miss ship boarding; unnamed sources, no official confirmation.

title: AWS, PHP2Shell exploitation in MadPot
finding: Honeypot telemetry saw a PHP2Shell exploit attempt 4 days before disclosure, proof-of-concept exploits about 12 hours before the embargo lifted, and several actors within hours of the patch (AWS sells detection and WAF products).

title: OpenAI, coordinated disclosure
finding: Says its model found the flaws before attackers, 'to our knowledge'; the AWS telemetry undercuts that head start.

title: Orosz, time to rethink software
finding: Infers that AI drives faster exploitation and the October 2026 incident cluster (opinion with incident relays).

title: Anthropic, using LLMs to secure source code
finding: Anthropic's scanning had disclosed 1,596 vulnerabilities, 97 known patched, as of 2026-05-22; one team's 40% false-positive rate came from findings with working proofs of concept that owners judged outside their threat model.

title: GitHub changelog, security validation for third-party agents
finding: GitHub runs CodeQL, advisory-database checks on new dependencies and secret scanning on third-party agent code by default, and claims hundreds of leaks and vulnerabilities prevented, unquantified.

title: Fucci et al., IEEE TSE 2017
finding: In a pre-LLM study of 39 professionals, test order made no significant difference while shorter, steadier cycles went with better quality and productivity, up to 14% better quality going from 50-minute to 8-minute cycles (small-to-medium effects, adjusted R2 about 0.1).

title: Boeckeler, TDD in the agent loop
finding: An agent (Sonnet 4.6) running TDD alone on a clear spec reached the same correctness and mutation score at 3x to 8.5x the tokens, and in every TDD run skipped RED, over-implemented or wrote tautological tests (5 batches, LLM judge, small experiment).

title: bdfinst, TDD vs non-TDD report
finding: Across 18 tasks, measured cost showed a 'cost advantage of test-after' of -9%, -55% and -8% by task size, baseline not stated.

title: Alonso, TDAD preprint
finding: On SWE-bench Verified with Qwen3-Coder 30B, a static test-impact map plus a short skill cut test-level regressions 70% (6.08% to 1.82%), while a procedural TDD prompt with no impact context raised them to 9.94%; single author, 100-125 instances, provisional.

title: SWE-CI
finding: Most models avoided regressions under 25% of the time.

title: Tornhill, Practices I abandoned with agents
finding: Testimony that agent-drafted, human-reviewed end-to-end tests are where the bulk of agentic gains came from, and that agents deleted tests or changed them to match wrong code.

title: Vaccari, Acceptance tests for AI-assisted development
finding: Recommends acceptance tests through in-memory adapters, converging independently on the approved-scenarios idea.

title: Beck on Pragmatic Engineer (TDD, AI agents)
finding: Calls TDD a 'superpower' against agent regressions, reports agents deleting or changing tests, and recalls a Facebook feature where TDD was a waste of time because the bugs that hurt were cross-subsystem (anecdote).

title: Beck, Augmented coding: beyond the vibes
finding: Human-enforced TDD with an agent took two failed attempts to calibrate.

title: Mock et al., XP 2024 workshop
finding: A chat model in a TDD loop edited an expected value instead of fixing the bug (5 participants, one case).

title: AlphaVerus, ICML 2025
finding: Without critique filters, assume(false) spread to every output of a prover-graded translation loop.

title: Approved Scenarios pattern
finding: Proposes approved scenarios and constrained test DSLs as hard-to-fake test formats.

title: AI Made Tools, TDD with AI
finding: Proposes a human writes plain-language test intent, AI expands it into test code, a human implements the production code and AI only refactors after (unbylined, low confidence).

title: Shen & Tamkin, Anthropic RCT
finding: In a vendor RCT (n=52, unreplicated), AI help gave quiz scores of 50% vs 67% (d=0.74), the biggest gap in debugging and no significant speed gain; in exploratory subgroups of 2 to 7 people, conceptual questions scored 65% or more and delegating under 40%.

title: Bastani et al., PNAS 2025
finding: Among about 1,000 students, unrestricted GPT lowered exam scores by 17%, while a hint-only tutor showed no exam penalty.

title: Kosmyna et al.
finding: In a preprint (n=54), 83% of LLM users couldn't quote their own essay minutes later, and writers who started without AI showed higher brain connectivity once they used it than the AI-first group ever reached.

title: Generation-effect meta-analysis
finding: Across 310 experiments, people recalled about 10 points more of what they generated themselves; general psychology, not AI-specific.

title: Fan et al.
finding: Among 234 students (self-report scales), human pairs scored significantly higher on collaboration and social presence than AI-assisted pairs or solo students.

title: Brynjolfsson et al.
finding: In a descriptive working paper, early-career jobs (ages 22-25) in AI-exposed roles were 19% below trend.

title: Liu, Christian et al., COLM 2026
finding: Across three experiments with 1,058 online participants, after 11 to 12 problems with a GPT-5 sidebar people tested without it solved fewer problems (d from -0.20 to -0.45) and skipped more in two of three, with the cost sitting with people who asked for direct answers; fractions and reading comprehension, not coding, and no durability data.

title: Bainbridge, 1983
finding: Automation research prescribes regular manual control to keep operator skills; it comes from industrial automation, not LLMs.

title: Yu et al.
finding: A position paper names the gap of when one agent's memory write must become visible to another, but measures nothing.

title: Spati, from Obsidian to enterprise company brain
finding: A blog with a demo, unmeasured, describes a design that blocks a conflicting memory write until a human decides.

title: Storey, cognitive debt
finding: Argues at least one human should fully understand each AI change, and that teams should record why, not what.

title: Storey, cognitive debt revisited
finding: Argues docs are not sufficient if they are not living artifacts.

title: Litt
finding: Proposes a 5-question quiz on a change before shipping it.

title: Würsch
finding: Proposes a comprehension commit gate for juniors.

title: antirez
finding: Cited for writing the message yourself as the ownership check.

title: goblindegook
finding: Argues pairing keeps intent in at least two heads.

title: James
finding: Argues pairing keeps intent in at least two heads.

title: Ronacher
finding: Argues agents remove the friction that synchronised people.

title: Spati, nobody knows anything anymore
finding: A growing note built on one anonymous account argues the bigger risk is whole teams no longer knowing the architecture or why choices were made.

title: Sahai
finding: Essay with a hypothetical example, arguing for more funding of the author's own field: at society scale, understanding must sit outside whoever proposes the system.

title: Tablan et al.
finding: In a vendor preprint, a shared memory raised LLM-judged code quality most for small models, 4.23 to 4.89 on a 5-point scale; the memory was seeded from the benchmark's own reference answers and no execution tests were reported.

title: Stannard
finding: On one bug fix (n=1), reading the diff, running the tests and questioning the agent was judging, not understanding; only re-implementing the fix gave understanding.

title: Karpathy (X post)
finding: Claims, without evidence, that a ladder of output formats from controlled English to diagrams, HTML pages and explainer videos makes oversight easier; the author is a former AI-education founder, an interest the post does not disclose.

title: Teeni & Katz, HHAI 2026
finding: In one developer's four months with Claude Code (163 episodes), decisions had to be re-explained every session and agreed rules decayed as conversations grew; it builds theory and gives no prevalence.

title: Rezazadeh et al.
finding: In a simulation of provenance-gated shared memory, accuracy went 0.27, then 0.61 after grants, then 0.37 after revocations; the paper has no proof of policy adherence, no attack test, and nothing on stale or conflicting entries.

title: Tiwari & Gupta
finding: A 2026 review says the provenance-gated memory approach ensures privacy, though the primary paper shows simulation only.

title: Letta
finding: Letta says an agent using a plain filesystem scored 74.0% on the LoCoMo chat-recall benchmark with GPT-4o mini, against 68.5% reported for Mem0's graph variant.

title: Chhikara et al. (Mem0)
finding: Mem0's own preprint scores full context at 72.90 and Mem0 at 66.88 on a judge metric; the benchmark tests conversation recall, not coding.

title: Atwood, rubber duck problem solving
finding: A 2012 essay with anecdotes argues explaining to a listener that cannot answer finds the gap.

title: Kaya, Feynman Technique
finding: Popular guide with no cited studies to writing a plain-words explanation for a novice.

title: Farnam Street, Feynman Technique
finding: Popular guide with no cited studies to writing a plain-words explanation for a novice; its steps differ from other guides.

title: Feynman lecture excerpt
finding: Physics, not code: two equivalent descriptions suggest different next changes, so being able to propose a change is a sharper test of understanding.

title: Horikawa et al., preprint
finding: Across 14,998 agentic commits (89.3% Codex-authored), low-level refactors were 35.8% vs a 24.4% human baseline and architectural refactors 43.0% vs 54.9%; design-smell counts showed no practically meaningful change (Cohen's d about -0.03).

title: Saba et al.
finding: A smaller, low-rigor comparison of refactoring tools on isolated snippets found wide model-to-model variance, with no human check on correctness.

title: Lyu et al., preprint
finding: In a 39-student, one-semester study, solo-AI was the worst of three conditions and human-plus-AI scored highest, directly disagreeing with Fan et al.

title: Smith, ASEE 2026
finding: A 10-study review found, corroborated across 2 studies, that after AI-paired programming students were more likely to believe they had a complete solution and no longer needed to learn to program.

title: James, The weight of AI on engineers
finding: Pairing with an agent is closer to reading someone's diff; freed time should go left of dev, to users and stakeholders.

title: HBR (2026)
finding: Describes cohort releases within a week.

title: Fowler site, refactoring economic benefit
finding: Splitting a large file cut tokens per change 83%; the agent couldn't choose refactorings unaided (n=1).

title: Laforgia
finding: When building is cheap, deciding what not to build is the skill.

title: Faler, the illusion of velocity
finding: Overproduction is Lean's worst waste.

title: Tornhill, compressed cognition
finding: Agents compress a day of decisions into one session.

title: Yegge, The AI vampire
finding: Argues for 3-4 hour workdays with agents.

title: Boag, Smashing Magazine
finding: Opinion, no data, about knowledge work in general (the author sells AI training): treat AI adoption as change management, start with enthusiasts, make failure safe, replace pages of rules with a few principles, and learn from shadow AI instead of banning it.

title: Sun, Bai & Dredze, Task Matters (Findings of ACL 2026)
finding: Peer-reviewed study showing that knowledge requirements shape LLM responses to context-memory conflict; not tested on code.

title: Shojaee et al., The Illusion of Thinking
finding: Apple preprint, The Illusion of Thinking, on early-2025 models.

title: Suprmind, AI hallucination rates
finding: Vendor aggregator of AI hallucination rates, secondhand.

title: Abitbol (Revolut), AI Engineer NYC 2026
caveat: self-reported; the productivity chart does not separate the model change from other causes
finding: A bank reports that strict budget limits made engineers ration tokens, and that self-hosting an open model for about 2,000 engineers cut its invoice to about a tenth and let them stop rationing; it gives no quality or full-cost figures.

title: Bache, Agentic AI breaks mob programming
finding: Agents break mob programming's timed rotation, intention-only talking and quiet-or-chaotic screen watching; she uses silent shared prompt writing, running commentary, reading the summary aloud and a retro that names the patterns used.

title: Farley, The industry is catching up
caveat: sells a course on this; most cited voices are secondhand
finding: Argues that when a machine writes the code, the human's job is an executable acceptance-test specification in four layers, written one scenario at a time, kept out of the agent's reach and approved by a person.

title: Grove, The New Code
caveat: argument by analogy, no measurements; written by an OpenAI employee
finding: Argues that code is a lossy projection of the specification, so teams should write and keep the spec, make it executable and test against it.

title: Böckeler, tdd-comparisons repository
caveat: two runs per condition; analysis written with an LLM
finding: The test-first prompt had no test-list step and told the agent not to design up front; one improved prompt produced both the best and the fourth-best of four runs.

title: Bache, The last year has changed everything about TDD
finding: Argues that the study finding no gain from TDD in the agent loop used a thin prompt (no test list, weak refactoring, no smell sensors), so the question is still open.

title: Bache, It doesn't help to push AI into a crappy process
finding: Says AI hung on a code-first process closes tickets faster but leaves the same weak tests and design, and describes the test-list, small-slice loop that experienced TDD practitioners use with agents.

title: Bache and Ördög, How to stop AI ruining your codebase
finding: Agents split a function only to satisfy a length limit; a hook that turns the linter's output into a short prompt saying what the smell means and how to fix it gave better refactors in the demo.

title: Suoniemi, prompt-vs-metric-eval
caveat: small: 18 functions, two models of one family, two smells; part of the gap is confounded
finding: Behavioural guidance gave about 83 percent genuine fixes on both models, against 29 and 6 percent for a bare linter message; one model did worse with the bare metric than with no guidance.

title: Bache and Selander, The most important AI coding advice
caveat: the tool author's self-report, no measured outcome
finding: Telling an agent to follow TDD failed because it skipped steps and over-implemented, so he blocks violations with hooks outside the prompt; he still reads every change.

title: Liao, Agents don't need memory
caveat: the maker's own tool, no measurement
finding: Argues agent memory should be a maintained Markdown brain that the agent reads before and updates after each task, not snippets retrieved from a vector store; he still trims it by hand.
